notes.meaning: King Herod Agrippa I began violently targeting members of the Christian church in Jerusalem. He did not do this out of true religious devotion, but to gain political popularity with the people. His powerful family had a long history of cruel rule, and he used that power to oppress the believers.

Herod had the apostle James, the brother of John, executed with a sword, which usually meant beheading. James was the first of the original twelve apostles to die as a martyr for his faith. His death fulfilled the words of Jesus, who had warned the brothers that they would share in His suffering.

When Herod saw how pleased the crowds and religious leaders were with the murder of James, he went further and arrested Peter too. This happened during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, a holy week when Jerusalem was packed with visitors for the Passover. Herod cared far more about pleasing people than doing what was right.

Herod locked Peter in prison and assigned sixteen soldiers to guard him in four rotating shifts. He waited until the Passover celebration ended because Jewish custom avoided holding public trials or executions during holy festivals. Herod planned to make a grand public spectacle of Peter's execution once the feast was over.

Peter was kept under heavy guard, but the church gathered together and prayed to God for him without stopping. Their prayers were deeply earnest, like someone stretching with all their strength for something they desperately need. Even though the believers lacked weapons or worldly influence, they knew God had the power to act.

On the very night before his planned trial and execution, Peter was sleeping soundly between two soldiers. He was handcuffed with two chains, while extra sentries guarded the prison entrance. Peter possessed such deep peace and trust in God that he could sleep calmly right in the face of death.

Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared, and a heavenly light filled the dark prison cell. The angel struck Peter on the side to wake him up and told him to get up quickly. At that exact moment, the heavy chains fell away from Peter's wrists without alerting the sleeping guards.

The angel told Peter to fasten his belt, put on his sandals, and wrap his outer coat around him. Peter obeyed every instruction calmly as the angel commanded him to follow. This orderly preparation showed that God was conducting a peaceful rescue rather than a panicked escape.

Peter got up and followed the angel out of the cell. The experience was so stunning and sudden that he did not realize it was actually taking place in the physical world. He assumed he was only seeing another spiritual vision.

The angel and Peter walked straight past the first and second guard posts without anyone stopping them. When they arrived at the heavy iron gate leading into the city, it swung open all by itself. After they had walked down one street together to safety, the angel suddenly vanished.

Standing alone in the cool night air, Peter finally came to his senses and realized what had happened. He knew for certain that the Lord had sent an angel to deliver him from Herod's grasp and from the execution the people expected. God stepped in at the final hour to save His servant's life.

Once Peter realized he was safe, he decided to walk to the home of Mary, the mother of John Mark. Her home was large enough to serve as a familiar gathering place for the believers in Jerusalem. Even late in the middle of the night, many Christians were gathered there praying for Peter.

Peter knocked at the entryway gate that led into the house. A young servant girl named Rhoda went to the gate to listen and find out who was knocking outside. The believers kept the doors locked tightly at night because they were afraid of their persecutors.

When Rhoda heard the man speaking, she recognized Peter's voice immediately. She was so overwhelmed with excitement that she forgot to open the gate to let him inside. Instead, she rushed back into the house to shout that Peter was standing at the entrance.

The people praying told Rhoda that she had completely lost her mind. When she kept insisting she was telling the truth, they guessed it must be Peter's guardian angel or a heavenly messenger instead. Even though they had been praying earnestly for his rescue, they struggled to believe God had answered their prayer so quickly.

While they were arguing inside, Peter stayed outside in the street and continued knocking. When they finally opened the door and saw him with their own eyes, they were utterly amazed. Their anxiety and sorrow were instantly replaced with overwhelming joy.

Peter signaled with his hand for everyone to be quiet so they would not attract the attention of hostile neighbors. He explained how the Lord had sent an angel to guide him safely out of the prison. After telling them to share the news with James and the rest of the church, Peter left for a safer, hidden place.

When morning came, there was widespread panic and confusion among the soldiers at the prison. Peter was gone from between the two guards, and nobody could explain how he had vanished. The soldiers were terrified because Roman law held guards responsible for escaped prisoners with their own lives.

Herod searched everywhere for Peter, and when the apostle could not be found, the king cross-examined the guards. Because they could not explain the escape, Herod ordered them to be put to death. After this public humiliation, Herod left Judea and went down to live in Caesarea.

Herod was in a bitter quarrel with the nearby coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon. Those cities relied heavily on food and grain shipped from Herod's territory, so they could not afford to remain his enemies. They bribed Blastus, the king's trusted personal servant, and came together to plead for peace.

On an appointed day of public festival, Herod put on his royal robes and sat upon his throne in the theater. His garments were woven with silver thread that dazzled the eyes of the crowd under the bright morning sun. From his high seat, the king delivered an impressive speech to the people.

The flattering crowd shouted back that Herod was speaking with the voice of a god and not a mortal man. The people used this false praise to flatter the king and secure his political favor. Herod gladly accepted their worship instead of stopping it.

An angel of the Lord struck Herod down immediately because he accepted worship that belongs only to God. He was overcome by excruciating internal agony, eaten by worms while still alive, and died. God showed that proud rulers who persecute His people are completely powerless before Him.

Even though a mighty king had tried to wipe out the early church, the message of the gospel continued to spread and multiply. Herod died in disgrace, but the church he attacked grew stronger every day. God proved that no earthly ruler or prison can stop His truth from reaching people.

Barnabas and Saul completed their mission of delivering relief funds to the needy believers in Jerusalem and returned to Antioch. When they headed back, they brought John Mark along to help them in their ministry. In spite of violent opposition, God continued to guide and expand the missionary work of His church.
